lead.t: Amoxicillin: Penicillin — First-line for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia — Rash, diarrhoea; allergy

b: Side effects of penicillins:
Hypersensitivity reactions — most important; range from maculopapular rash → urticaria → anaphylaxis; cross-reactivity with cephalosporins is low (~1–2%) but must be considered
Ampicillin rash — non-allergic maculopapular rash occurring in patients with EBV infectious mononucleosis; NOT a true penicillin allergy
Diarrhoea — especially amoxicillin; risk of C. difficile colitis
Neurotoxicity — seizures at very high IV doses (especially in renal failure)

Amoxicillin: Penicillin — Alternative for a purulent exacerbation — Rash, diarrhoea, allergy
Co-amoxiclav: Penicillin plus β-lactamase inhibitor — Resistant organisms or pneumonia — Diarrhoea, liver injury
Amoxicillin: Penicillin — Exacerbation with Haemophilus or pneumococcus (14 days) — Rash, diarrhoea

qs.q: A patient with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia is prescribed oral amoxicillin 500 mg 8-hourly. If the patient has a documented penicillin allergy, which alternative oral antibiotic regimen is recommended?
qs.e: For penicillin-allergic patients with uncomplicated CAP, clarithromycin 500 mg 12-hourly or erythromycin 500 mg 6-hourly is recommended. Co-amoxiclav and ceftriaxone contain beta-lactam rings that may cross-react in penicillin allergies.

qs.q: What is the recommended treatment regimen for a patient diagnosed with primary or secondary syphilis who is allergic to penicillin?
o: Benzathine penicillin administered as a three-dose course
Doxycycline taken orally for a duration of two weeks
Ceftriaxone administered daily for a total of seven days
A single intramuscular dose of azithromycin given once
qs.e: For patients with primary or secondary syphilis who are allergic to the first-line benzathine penicillin, oral doxycycline for 2 weeks is the recommended alternative. Benzathine penicillin is instead reserved for non-allergic individuals or late-stage disease.

qs.q: What is the most common mechanism by which bacteria develop resistance to penicillin-type drugs?
o: Producing beta-lactamase enzymes that break down the drug
Modifying the structural target that the antibiotic binds
Developing active efflux pumps to expel the medication
Altering cell wall permeability to block drug entry
qs.e: Beta-lactamase production is the most common bacterial resistance mechanism, involving enzymes that break down penicillin-type drugs before they can act. Altered drug targets and efflux pumps are alternative mechanisms.

qs.q: A 4-year-old child with hereditary spherocytosis undergoes a total splenectomy. For how long should prophylactic penicillin therapy be continued postoperatively?
o: For the first 14 days after surgery
Until age 10 and at least 5 years
Until age 5 and at least 2 years
For the first 6 months after surgery
qs.e: Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended until at least age 5 and for a minimum of 2 years post-splenectomy to prevent overwhelming infection. A 14-day course is insufficient for providing adequate long-term protection against encapsulated organisms.

qs.q: A patient with infective endocarditis caused by penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus viridans is planned for treatment. Which of the following is an acceptable first-line antibiotic regimen?
o: Single dose oral amoxicillin for 2 weeks
qs.e: Penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus Viridans or Bovis can be treated with once daily ceftriaxone (or IV penicillin G or IV amoxicillin) for 4 weeks, or ceftriaxone for 2 weeks followed by other options. Flucloxacillin is instead used for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus.

qs.q: What is the recommended antibiotic treatment when a strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae shows high penicillin resistance?
qs.e: If Streptococcus pneumoniae shows high penicillin resistance, it is likely to be resistant to penicillins, cephalosporins, and macrolides; therefore, Vancomycin should be given instead.

qs.q: Which specific penicillin derivative is indicated exclusively for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections due to its penicillinase resistance?
qs.e: Flucloxacillin is penicillinase-resistant and specifically used for MSSA skin, bone, and endocarditis infections. Benzylpenicillin is a narrow-spectrum agent used for streptococci and other pathogens rather than MSSA.

qs.q: Which antimicrobial agent is structurally classified as a monobactam, acts exclusively on Gram-negative bacteria, and is safe to use in patients with penicillin allergies?
qs.e: Aztreonam is a monobactam with activity limited strictly to Gram-negative organisms and has minimal cross-reactivity, making it safe in penicillin allergies. Vancomycin and daptomycin are exclusively active against Gram-positive bacteria.

ai.title: Penicillins in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Penicillins are first‑line agents for many childhood infections in low‑resource settings. Clinicians must recognise efficacy, spectrum, and common adverse reactions, and be alert to cross‑reactivity and local resistance patterns.

sections.p: Penicillins are β‑lactam antibiotics that inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis. In children they are used for a range of infections from otitis media to pneumonia and meningitis. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple tests when available.
b: Broad spectrum against Gram‑positive cocci; limited Gram‑negative activity unless combined with a β‑lactamase inhibitor.

sections.p: Severity is judged by clinical signs: mild (e.g., uncomplicated otitis media), moderate (community‑acquired pneumonia), severe (sepsis, meningitis).
b: Mild: fever <38.5°C, no respiratory distress. Moderate: tachypnoea, chest indrawing. Severe: lethargy, hypotension, altered consciousness.

sections.p: Common pathogens in East Africa include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (non‑typeable), and Staphylococcus aureus. In malaria‑endemic areas, bacterial sepsis may coexist with parasitemia.
b: S. pneumoniae – first choice for pneumonia.
H. influenzae – treat with amoxicillin or co‑amoxiclav if β‑lactamase production suspected.

sections.p: Infections treated with penicillins present with typical bacterial signs: fever, local inflammation, purulent drainage. In meningitis, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered sensorium are key.
b: Otitis media – ear pain, bulging tympanic membrane.
Pneumonia – cough, tachypnoea, chest indrawing.

sections.p: Lab tests are limited; use what is available.
b: If cultures unavailable, start empiric penicillin based on local guidelines.

t.a: Rapid antigen test for S. pneumoniae
t.b: Detects pneumococcal antigen in urine; positive supports diagnosis of pneumonia.
Identifies bacteremia; guides antibiotic choice if resistant.
Elevated in bacterial infection; helps differentiate from viral.
Shows infiltrates; confirms pneumonia when available.
Diagnoses bacterial meningitis; opening pressure and CSF Gram stain guide therapy.

sections.p: Watch for signs of severe infection, allergic reaction, or treatment failure.
b: Anaphylaxis – sudden hypotension, urticaria, bronchospasm.
Severe diarrhoea – possible C. difficile colitis.
Persistent fever after 48h – consider resistance or alternative diagnosis.

sections.p: Treat the infection first, then supportive care. Penicillins are chosen for their safety profile, low cost, and local efficacy.
Ensure completion of therapy, monitor for adverse effects, and counsel on hand hygiene and vaccination.
b: Re‑evaluate at 48–72h; if no improvement, switch to broader therapy.
Vaccinate against S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae type b to reduce incidence.

sections.p: Other β‑lactams and non‑antibiotic causes of similar symptoms.
b: Cephalosporins – similar spectrum but higher cross‑reactivity risk.
Viral infections – may mimic bacterial pneumonia but lack purulent drainage.

sections.p: Low sensitivity of rapid tests and delayed culture results can mask resistance.
b: A negative rapid antigen test does not exclude pneumococcal pneumonia.
Normal CRP can occur in early bacterial infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), persistent fever >48h despite therapy, signs of sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension), neurological deterioration (in meningitis).

faq.q: What is the most common penicillin allergy sign in children?
faq.a: A maculopapular rash that may appear 1–2 days after starting the drug.

faq.q: When is co‑amoxiclav preferred over amoxicillin?
faq.a: When β‑lactamase production is suspected, in severe infections, or when covering anaerobes.

faq.q: Can a child with EBV mononucleosis safely receive ampicillin?
faq.a: Yes; the rash is a non‑allergic reaction and does not indicate true allergy.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with cough and fever presents with chest indrawing. What is the first antibiotic choice? — Amoxicillin, as first‑line for community‑acquired pneumonia in children.
A child develops a maculopapular rash 48h after starting amoxicillin. What is the next step? — Continue therapy; the rash is likely a benign reaction, not an allergy.
A 4‑year‑old with suspected meningitis is started on benzylpenicillin. What adjunct therapy is recommended? — Metronidazole to cover anaerobes in the meninges.
A child with pneumonia does not improve after 48h on amoxicillin. What is the likely cause? — Possible β‑lactamase–producing organism; switch to co‑amoxiclav.
A child presents with severe diarrhoea after starting amoxicillin. What complication should be considered? — C. difficile colitis, especially if the child has renal impairment.
A child with a penicillin allergy history is needed for urgent surgery. What is the safest antibiotic? — Cefazolin, given low cross‑reactivity (~1–2%).
A child in a malaria‑endemic area has fever and purulent sputum. What additional test should you consider? — Rapid malaria test to rule out concurrent malaria.
A child with suspected bacterial sepsis has a normal CRP but persistent fever. What should you do? — Obtain blood cultures and consider broadening empiric therapy.
